title: AI Scribe or Templates? What Each One Writes in a PT Clinic
summary: An AI scribe for physical therapy drafts your evals; templates save the rest. See what each tool actually writes across a typical day in a PT clinic.
body_markdown:
## Where the typing in a PT clinic actually goes


When it comes to physical therapy documentation, an AI scribe can save real time on evaluations, where it turns the conversation in the room into a draft note. However, much of the rest of a PT clinic's typing, such as daily notes, PTA follow-ups, goals and patient messages, is often quicker to type yourself. To see where the typing burden really lies in a physical therapy practice, look at how much text is produced on a typical day. This is the stream of documentation and communication a busy outpatient clinic generates between the first patient and close:


- One or two evals, each with a history, objective measures, goals and a plan of care
- A dozen or more daily notes, many of them written by a PTA
- A progress note coming due, with goals to update and a skilled-need line for the next visits
- Home exercise program updates and instructions
- Reminders, cancellations and texts to patients about their next appointment


An AI scribe captures what was said in the room, but the short daily notes and the back-and-forth between the clinic and the patient still consume a lot of staff time.


## What an AI scribe covers well: the evaluation conversation


AI scribes have earned their place in the evaluation. The PT talks to the patient as usual while the scribe listens and drafts the subjective and much of the objective: the history, what the patient reported, and what was found during the examination. The transcribed text is then structured into the note.


The evaluation is where AI scribes are the most helpful. A long conversation turns into a ready draft. Clinicians who use an AI scribe for evals often report a noticeable drop in their end-of-day backlog. Some describe eval documentation that used to take a quarter of an hour or more now taking about five minutes. Instead of sitting after the last patient trying to reconstruct a history from memory, they find the drafts already waiting in their EMR.


Audio quality varies from room to room, and drafting style differs across software. But the main function stays the same: the AI scribe filters out small talk from the clinical dialogue and produces a draft in a standard format, so the PT can focus on the patient rather than the keyboard during the eval.


## Where PTs still need to edit after an AI scribe


Evaluations aren't the only notes a PT writes, and daily notes are a different job. A routine follow-up visit has little conversation worth transcribing and a lot of specific numbers: sets, reps, load, minutes, the patient's response and progress toward goals. Much of the work happens between exercises, where there is no conversation for a scribe to listen to.


### Do AI scribes save time on PT daily notes?


For many PTs and PTAs, not much. On a short daily note, editing a draft can take as long as typing it. Sometimes a long paragraph has to be cut down to the few lines that matter, which some find slower than typing a concise note themselves.

## You still review every note


Clinics that use a scribe follow the same workflow: the tool generates a draft, and the PT reads it, corrects anything that needs it, and signs it. PTs who use AI scribes like them, but they also recommend reviewing every draft. Whoever drafted the note, the therapist is still the one who checks and adjusts it.


The review itself becomes a repetitive bottleneck. Whether the PT is trimming a paragraph or adding the plan for next visit, the corrections follow familiar patterns. PTs end up typing the same tolerance line, the same skilled-need sentence and the same plan again and again.


Those repeated parts are faster to check when the wording is your own and always the same. You read your own sentence and know it says what you mean; only that day's details need a second look.


This is where Text Blaze fits in. A PT can type a shortcut such as /tol to drop their standard tolerance line into the draft and speed up the review. PTs can save their own phrasing or start from ready-made templates, and a pop-up lets them fill in the details that change from visit to visit.


## Using both: a worked example of one follow-up visit


Here's how an AI scribe and saved snippets work together during a routine follow-up: a patient on visit eight of rehab after a total knee replacement.


**Check-in:** The patient tells the PT how the knee has felt since the last visit. If the scribe is running, this is the part it can draft, the subjective in the patient's own words.


**In the gym:** The patient works through the exercises: quad sets, heel slides, terminal knee extension with a band, and step-ups at 3 x 10 on a 6-inch step. Knee flexion measures 110 degrees, up from 102 at visit four. The conversation is short and happens between sets, so there is little for a scribe to draft.


**Writing the daily note:** The PT types /ptsoap, from the free[Physical Therapy SOAP Note & Daily Note Templates](https://text.blaze.today/marketplace/templates/physical-therapy-soap-note-templates) , and a Text Blaze pop-up opens with boxes for pain, exercises with sets and reps, and minutes per timed code. The PT fills in today's numbers and types /tol to add the tolerance line. The PT reads the note once and signs it.


**Home program:** The PT adds step-ups to the home exercise program with a saved snippet for the patient's instructions, filling in the sets, reps and how often. The wording is the same for every patient doing step-ups and only the numbers change.


**Follow-up:** Before the patient leaves, the front desk uses a snippet to text them the time of their next appointment and a reminder to bring their home program sheet.


The scribe could help with the subjective. The other steps of this visit were handled by saved snippets and keyboard shortcuts.
